lessons.title: Animal products and when they are ready
lessons.html:
Animal products and when they are ready

Animal products are things we take from animals to use or sell. Some products come from live animals, and some come after slaughter.

Names and where they come from

ProductAnimalUse
MilkDairy cows, goatsDrinking, cheese, maas
EggsHensFood
WoolSheep, such as MerinoClothes, blankets
MohairAngora goatsFine cloth
HoneyBeesFood
Meat, hides, skinsCattle, sheep, goats, pigs, chickensFood, leather
ManureAll livestockFertiliser, compost

These products earn money for the farm. South Africa is one of the large producers of mohair and wool in the world.

Signs that a product is ready

  • Milk: the cow has calved and is in milk; her udder is full at milking time. Milk from a cow that has just calved (colostrum) goes to the calf.
  • Eggs: hens lay daily; eggs are ready to collect at set times.
  • Wool: the fleece has grown to the right length, usually after about a year for Merino sheep. The shearing date is set by the farmer.
  • Honey: the bees have capped the honey cells with wax.
  • Animals for slaughter: they have reached the right weight and condition.

Do not harvest when

  • The animal has been treated with medicine and the withdrawal period on the label has not passed. Milk, eggs and meat may then not be sold.
  • The animal is sick.
  • The product is dirty or spoiled.

Your supervisor will tell you which animals are ready and which are being treated. Treated animals are often marked, for example with a coloured leg band or spray mark. Learn the farm's marks so you never harvest from a treated animal by mistake.

lessons.title: Harvesting milk, eggs and wool correctly
lessons.html:
Harvesting milk, eggs and wool correctly

Milking

  1. Bring cows calmly to the milking shed. Do not hit or shout.
  2. Wash your hands and wear clean clothes.
  3. Clean and dry the teats.
  4. Strip a few squirts from each teat into a strip cup and look for clots or blood. These are signs of mastitis. Report it.
  5. Put on the milking machine or milk by hand.
  6. Take off the cups when milk flow stops. Do not over-milk.
  7. Dip teats in teat dip after milking.
  8. Cool the milk quickly in the bulk tank.
  9. Keep milk from treated cows separate, as marked, and do not put it in the tank.

Collecting eggs

  • Collect at the set times, with clean hands.
  • Place eggs gently in trays, pointed end down.
  • Keep cracked and dirty eggs apart.
  • Take eggs to a cool egg room.

Shearing sheep

  • Shearing is done by trained shearers. You may help by bringing sheep, keeping the floor clean and picking up fleeces.
  • Keep sheep dry before shearing; wet wool cannot be packed.
  • Throw the fleece onto the table so it can be skirted and classed.
  • Keep wool clean of straw, plastic and string.

Safety and animal care

  • Cows can kick. Stand to the side, move slowly and speak calmly.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty to animals an offence. Handle animals gently.
  • Wash hands after handling animals. Cover cuts.

Key points

  • Milk, eggs, wool, mohair, honey, meat, hides and manure are animal products.
  • Each product has signs that show it is ready.
  • Never sell products from treated animals before the withdrawal period ends.
  • Clean hands and gentle handling protect product quality.
  • Report signs of mastitis such as clots in milk.
